newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia cuts out the fat from its oil exports.
newsitem.headline: Russia cuts out the fat from its oil exports.

text.p: Russian oil exporters lost one of their biggest perks on Wednesday when the Kremlin scrapped a scheme that allowed them to earn easy cash from sending black gold abroad in exchange for financing pet state projects.
But energy analysts said abolishing the system, known as federal programmes, would not alter the amount of Russian oil pumped to world markets.

First Deputy Prime Minister Boris Nemtsov, who is also energy minister, said President Boris Yeltsin had signed a decree abolishing the scheme, saying there were better ways for the state to raise cash.
The programmes accounted for about 15 percent of Russia's total crude oil exports last year of 2.51 million barrels per day (bpd), including 2.1 million bpd to the West.

Their elimination is a victory for Russian oil producers over traders and middlemen and could lead to the transparency and efficiency markets want to see in Russia, the world's third largest oil producer.
"It's basically a move against oil traders and third parties dealing in oil," said Renaissance Capital energy analyst Alexei Kokin.
Traders have dominated the federal programmes, enraging producers, who say they need to export as much as possible through Russia's cramped pipelines if they are to survive.

Russia's total oil export capacity is around 100-120 million tonnes (1.73-2.0 million bpd), but most of the spare capacity is on the Druzhba (Friendship) pipeline to Eastern Europe, where lower demand and diversification have set in.
That means fierce competition for pipeline space -- and, with the elimination of the programmes, more room for producers.
"It (the scrapping) will squeeze out the independent middleman but it won't squeeze out those who know the market," said Stephen O'Sullivan, oil and gas director at MC Securities.

Nemtsov told a closed briefing, a tape recording of which was obtained by Reuters, that eliminating the programmes would allow producers to take charge of their exports and thus pay more oil revenues into the budget.
Russian oil exports were worth $13 billion last year, and the new reformist cabinet is keen to use taxes from the money judiciously to keep reforms on track.
"The point of the decree is to scrap the programme and to give oil companies the possibility to export independently," Nemtsov said.

Exports for state needs, a relic of the Soviet planned economy era, were a windfall when Russia's domestic oil prices were one third of world prices. Many companies simply sold the oil to offshore affiliates at artificially low prices and billed the Russian government for the difference.
But with domestic oil prices now closer to world levels, the game had changed, making securing oil cheaply on the home market, not just exporting it, one of the keys to success.
Federal programmes were used to finance government pet projects ranging from satellite launches from the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan to repainting the Kremlin for holidays.
"You probably know that a lot of oil was supplied for state needs, and to our great regret, the effectiveness of the programmes was very low," Nemtsov said.
Now the Kremlin has bigger priorities, like paying salaries to soldiers and making sure market economy reforms do not derail over popular dissatisfaction with the pain of change.
The big fish moved even before the Kremlin net closed, since the government has slowly reduced the amount of export pipeline space available under the programmes in recent years.
"The smart traders have moved into other things," said a senior Russian oil trader.

Scrapping the programmes is part of Moscow's efforts to liberalise oil exports. Russia has come a long way since the days of quotas and licences, a system many viewed as open to influence-peddling, inefficiency and corruption.
Before 1995, only 20 or so companies -- few of them producers and many unrelated to the energy sector, like the Afghan War Veterans' group -- were allowed to export oil.
Moscow has scrapped export tariff-based controls but still needs a revamped system of access to cramped pipelines.
"The decree (scrapping the programmes) is important because of the idea that access to pipelines should be granted on a pro-rata basis according to production rates," Kokin said.

Nemtsov pointed to other benefits, saying Russian oil companies could pay off the equivalent of $521 million in tax arrears directly into the budget, instead of into accounts for pet state projects, by 1998.
